questions.question: How do you implement binary search in Go?
questions.title: Binary Search Go
questions.direct_answer: Sorted array, target, halve the range: mid, compare, adjust lo/hi. Returns the index or -1. O(log n). Verified: binarySearch([1,3,5,7,9,11,13], 7) = 3.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Sorted array, target, halve the range: mid, compare, adjust lo/hi. Returns the index or -1. O(log n). Verified: binarySearch([1,3,5,7,9,11,13], 7) = 3.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[sorted array] --> L0[lo=0, hi=n-1]
    L0 --> M[mid = lo + hi-lo/2]
    M --> EQ{arr[mid] == target?}
    EQ -->|yes| R[return mid]
    EQ -->|arr[mid] < target| L1[lo = mid+1]
    EQ -->|arr[mid] > target| H1[hi = mid-1]
    L1 --> M
    H1 --> M
    L0 --> EMPTY[lo > hi] --> N[return -1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The loop invariants, formally: (1) if target is in the array, its index is always in [lo, hi]; (2) each iteration either returns or strictly decreases hi - lo. Together: termination with correctness. The off-by-one bugs are always violations of (1) or (2) — including mid in the next range (non-termination) or excluding the answer (missed finds).

The binary-search-on-answer pattern (the interview extension): when the PREDICATE is monotonic rather than the array — 'find the smallest capacity that works' — the same loop operates over the answer space. sort.Search(n, func(i int) bool { return feasible(i) }) is exactly this — the generalization that makes binary search a design tool, not just a sorted-array lookup.

The precision: the search does exactly ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons in the worst case — for 1M elements, ~20 comparisons. The math: each comparison splits the remaining range in half; halving k times from n leaves n/2^k; the range hits 0 in k = log2(n) steps.
